How Nevada values a house for tax

Nevada property tax starts with the county assessor, an elected official who finds, lists and values the real and personal property in the county. The state Department of Taxation oversees the system, and its guide to the property tax explains the method. The number on your bill begins at the county level.

The state defines taxable value as land at full cash value plus improvements at replacement cost new, less depreciation. In plain terms, the lot is priced as if sold, while the structure is priced by rebuilding cost with a deduction for age and wear. A market sale price follows a different logic, which is why the assessor's number and a buyer's offer can differ.

Only part of taxable value is taxed. NRS 361.225 sets assessment at 35 percent of taxable value for all taxable property, and each owner receives a notice of assessed value as the tax roll is prepared.

  • Land: full cash value, close to market value for the lot.
  • Improvements: replacement cost new, minus depreciation.
  • Assessed value: 35 percent of the sum of the two.
  • Tax bill: assessed value times the combined local rate, less any abatement.

Caps on how much the tax can rise

Two limits apply: a ceiling on the total tax rate, and an abatement that holds down year-over-year increases on homes.

NRS 361.453 caps the total ad valorem levy for all public purposes at $3.64 on each $100 of assessed valuation, with listed exceptions. The Legislature set that rate in 1979 and later added $0.02 for state debt, bringing the total to $3.66. The rate you pay varies with the parcel's location, so check your own bill.

The abatement is in NRS 361.4723. Lawmakers there declared an increase beyond 3 percent a hardship and ordered a partial abatement for an owner-occupied single-family residence. For those homes, one year's bill may climb no more than 3 percent above the previous levy. A general abatement of up to 8 percent covers other parcels.

Tax featureRule
Assessment ratio35 percent of taxable value (NRS 361.225)
Total levy ceiling$3.64 per $100 of assessed value, with exceptions (NRS 361.453)
Primary residence abatementBill cannot rise more than 3 percent over the prior year (NRS 361.4723)
Other parcelsGeneral abatement of up to 8 percent

Due dates and penalties

NRS 361.483 lets an owner split a bill of more than $100 into four roughly equal installments. Payments fall on the third Monday of August, then the first Monday of October, January and March. Treasurers send bills by early August.

  • One installment unpaid 10 days after its due date: 4 percent penalty.
  • Two installments unpaid: 5 percent on the two installments due.
  • Three installments unpaid: 6 percent on the three installments due.
  • Full amount unpaid 10 days after the first Monday of March: 7 percent of the full amount.

Anyone penalized should be told about NRS 361.4835. It allows a county treasurer or assessor to forgive some or all of a late penalty and interest in the situations it lists. Ask the treasurer before you treat a penalty as final.

What happens when taxes go unpaid?

Unpaid tax stays with the house. NRS 361.450 makes each property tax a perpetual lien until paid, ranking above every other lien, claim, encumbrance and title, even ones filed or perfected earlier. It attaches July 1 of the levy year.

When a bill remains open past the first Monday in June, the county holds the property for a two-year redemption period. The owner can redeem during those years by paying taxes, penalties, costs and 10 percent annual interest. With no payment, the property is deeded to the county treasurer as trustee and may go to public auction. Our Nevada tax sale guide covers that process in detail.

Two things follow in practice. Any buyer or title company will want unpaid tax cleared at closing. Waiting also costs money, since penalties and certificate interest keep growing each month.

Tax checks before you list

Pull three documents first: your newest tax bill, your notice of assessed value, and the treasurer's account record for the parcel.

  1. Match each installment to a payment. Bills mailed to an old address or to a lender can leave a balance open for months.
  2. Check whether the abatement applies. The residence must be the owner's designated primary residence and cannot be rented or made available for exclusive occupancy by anyone other than the owner and family (NRS 361.4723).
  3. Check the assessor's numbers against the house you own. A county board appeal under NRS 361.357 cannot increase your taxable value. File by January 15, after first completing the assessor's form.
  4. Ask whether special assessments are attached. NRS 361.450 treats assessments under chapter 271 as liens with the same priority as tax.

For an inherited house, confirm whose name is on the roll. A bill still addressed to a deceased owner can go delinquent unnoticed.

Transfer tax when a house sells

Each deed carries a real property transfer tax, and the rate turns on county population. Under NRS 375.020 it is $1.25 per $500 of value in counties of 700,000 or more people and 65 cents per $500 elsewhere, once the value conveyed tops $100.

NRS 375.060 requires a declaration of value form, and the tax is computed from the value on it. This statute covers just the base tax, so ask the county recorder about local add-ons.

Who pays is a contract term, so the purchase agreement should say. On a typical settlement statement you will see the transfer tax, prorated property tax and any open delinquency.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with property tax owing

A house with tax owing can sell, as long as the title company can clear the lien at closing, usually by paying the balance from the sale proceeds.

Cash buyers handle this often because they do not wait on a lender's underwriting. The steps are the same either way: get a payoff figure from the county treasurer, include penalties and interest to the closing date, and give the escrow officer time to confirm the amount. If a trustee certificate has already been issued, redemption costs more, since it adds interest at 10 percent a year plus costs.

Timing matters most when an auction is near. Nevada lets an owner, a lender and a person holding a contract to purchase redeem until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale (NRS 361.585). A buyer under contract can protect the deal that way, but only if the money moves in time. We make offers on Nevada houses as-is, and we can review a tax bill with you before you decide anything.

Frequently asked questions

Who sets my Nevada property tax rate?

Several local bodies do, within the state ceiling. The total levy for all public purposes cannot exceed $3.64 per $100 of assessed value except as the statute allows (NRS 361.453). The county assessor sets the value and the county treasurer sends the bill.

What is the assessed value of a Nevada house?

It is 35 percent of taxable value under NRS 361.225. Taxable value is the land's full cash value plus the replacement cost of improvements less depreciation.

Can I pay Nevada property tax in installments?

Yes, if the bill is over $100. The four installments fall due the third Monday of August, then the first Mondays of October, January and March (NRS 361.483). Penalties start at 4 percent for one late installment.

Does a tax lien come ahead of other liens in Nevada?

Yes. Under NRS 361.450 the property tax lien is superior to all other liens, claims and encumbrances, whether or not the other lien was filed first.

Is there a limit on how much my Nevada home tax can increase?

For an owner-occupied single-family primary residence, the partial abatement in NRS 361.4723 holds the yearly increase to 3 percent. Other property has a general abatement of up to 8 percent.

What the Nevada homestead exemption protects

The exemption shields a home from forced sale to pay most creditors, up to a fixed amount of equity. NRS 115.010 says a homestead is not subject to forced sale on execution or any final court process. The shield covers equity of $605,000, unless allodial title has been established and not relinquished.

It is a creditor-protection rule, separate from property tax relief. NRS 115.080 makes clear that nothing in the chapter exempts property from sale for taxes. Owners who want a smaller tax bill should look at the abatement and exemption programs near the end of this page.

The statute defines equity. It is the fair market value of the property minus the liens the exemption does not protect against, including mortgages and certain other liens. Only what is left counts against the $605,000 limit.

What counts as a homestead

NRS 115.005 recognizes three kinds: land with a dwelling and its appurtenances, a mobile home whether or not the claimant owns the land under it, and a condominium or common-interest unit with its share of common elements. Both spouses, either spouse, or a single person can make the claim.

A married claimant's declaration must say the claimants are married and live on the premises with their family or with the people they support. Every declaration must state an intention to use and claim the property as a homestead. If the property is one spouse's separate property, both spouses must join in signing and acknowledging the declaration.

Under NRS 115.030, tenants in common may each declare a homestead in their own share, subject to the co-owners' right to force a partition. A trustee can claim a homestead for the person who created the trust, or for beneficiaries, when those people live in the property.

Filing a homestead declaration

Sign the declaration, have it acknowledged, and record it with the county recorder where the property sits. The acknowledgment and recording are the same as for a deed.

The Real Estate Division of the Department of Business and Industry prescribes a form. NRS 115.025 requires it to be free at the Division's offices and website and at every county recorder's office. You do not have to use it, but it carries the required statements.

  • Choose the property you actually live in and describe it in the declaration.
  • Sign it and have the signature acknowledged before a notary.
  • Record it with the county recorder. The recorder may charge a recording fee, though the statute allows recording without one.
  • Keep a certified copy with your closing and estate papers.

The law also protects consumers from paid solicitors. Anyone who charges a fee to record your declaration must first hand you a bold-type notice saying you can record it yourself. A violation is a misdemeanor under NRS 115.020.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Debts that can still reach a homestead

Several claims fall outside the exemption. NRS 115.010 says the protection does not extend to process enforcing the debt for buying the property, for improvements to it including a mechanic's lien, for legal taxes, or for a mortgage or deed of trust, including a second mortgage, refinance, line of credit or home equity loan.

Association liens are also outside it. When an owner takes property subject to recorded restrictions, the owner has given prior consent to a lien under NRS 116.3116 or 117.070, and the exemption does not stand in its way. NRS 115.090 adds that nothing in the chapter blocks recovery of Medicaid money owed to the Nevada Health Authority through a lien.

Type of claimReaches a homestead?
General unsecured judgmentProtected up to $605,000 of equity
Mortgage, deed of trust, HELOCYes
Purchase price or improvement debt, mechanic's lienYes
Property taxesYes
Association lienYes
Medicaid recovery lienYes

Allodial title changes some of this, because the statute then extends the exemption to those debts unless a waiver was signed. That route is rare and has its own rules, so get legal advice before relying on it.

Selling a homestead and who must sign

A homestead can be sold. The exemption does not stop the owner from conveying it. What trips people up is the signatures: under NRS 115.040, a mortgage or alienation made to secure a loan is invalid unless both spouses sign and acknowledge it, where the marriage exists.

A homestead is also not treated as abandoned without a written declaration of abandonment. Both spouses, or the single claimant, sign and acknowledge it, and it is recorded in the same office as the original declaration. If you move out and want the claim off the record, that is the document to record.

If a spouse cannot join because of incapacity, NRS 115.070 lets the owner petition the district court for a license to convey by the owner's sole deed, on at least 20 days' notice to the spouse's kindred living in the state. The court can also direct how the proceeds are invested to protect the spouse.

When a declaration is on record, tell the escrow officer early, so the abandonment and signature questions are settled before the closing date.

Sale proceeds under the homestead law

In a forced sale, the first $605,000 goes to the homeowner, and that money stays protected only if it is reinvested promptly. NRS 115.050 covers the case where a creditor swears equity exceeds $605,000 and the court appoints three appraisers. If the property cannot be divided, it is sold, no bid under $605,000 may be accepted, and $605,000 is paid to the debtor.

NRS 115.055 sets the clock for that money. It is exempt from execution only if reinvested in another property of like kind for which a homestead will be declared. The new property must be identified within 45 days after the homestead sale and possessed within 180 days.

Those deadlines are written for execution sales. An ordinary voluntary sale to a buyer is a different situation, so ask an attorney how the rule applies to you before treating the 45 and 180 day dates as your own.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

When the owner dies

A declared homestead held as community property is treated as held with a right of survivorship, so on the first death the property vests in the survivor. NRS 115.060 adds that the exemption continues without a new filing as to debts existing against the spouses until the survivor dies.

For a single owner, the exemption continues as to debts existing at death and as to later debts of a relative by blood or marriage who lived in the house and keeps living there. NRS 146.010 lets a surviving spouse or minor children stay in possession of the homestead, and NRS 146.020 allows a court to set it apart. A homestead selected and recorded by the spouses during the marriage vests absolutely in the survivor under NRS 146.050, unless NRS 115.060 requires otherwise.

Heirs who want to sell an inherited house should read our probate guide first, because letters or a court order may be needed.

Property tax relief is a separate matter

Nevada limits the yearly rise in tax on a primary residence through a partial abatement. NRS 361.4723 applies a 3 percent cap, and only one property in the state can be your chosen primary residence. A cap of up to 8 percent applies to homes that are not owner occupied.

Exemptions also exist for surviving spouses, blind persons and people with military service or a service-related disability, claimed through the county assessor. Taxes are paid in four installments, due the third Monday of August, the first Monday of October, the first Monday of January and the first Monday of March. An assessment can be appealed to the County Board of Equalization, usually in January.

A seller who is behind on taxes should know the homestead does not protect against a tax sale. Paying from sale proceeds at closing is often the cleanest fix, and the escrow officer will order the balance from the county.

Frequently asked questions

How much is the Nevada homestead exemption?

It protects up to $605,000 of equity under NRS 115.010, unless allodial title has been established and not relinquished. The limit applies to equity after the liens the exemption does not cover, not to the home's market value.

Is the Nevada homestead exemption a property tax break?

No. It protects the home from forced sale to creditors, and NRS 115.080 says the chapter does not exempt property from sale for taxes. Tax relief comes from the 3 percent abatement and the exemptions for surviving spouses and similar groups.

Do I have to file a homestead declaration in Nevada?

The protection arises from a declaration that is signed, acknowledged and recorded with the county recorder. The Real Estate Division's form is free at the Division and every county recorder, and you can record it yourself.

Can a spouse refuse to sign when I sell a homestead?

A mortgage or other alienation to secure a debt on a homestead is invalid without both spouses' signatures under NRS 115.040. If one spouse cannot join because of incapacity, NRS 115.070 provides a court license to convey by the owner's sole deed.

Does the homestead protect my house from a mortgage foreclosure?

No. NRS 115.010 says the exemption does not reach a mortgage or deed of trust, including second mortgages, refinances, lines of credit and home equity loans. Purchase money debt, mechanic's liens, taxes and association liens are also outside it.

Nevada's deed upon death

Nevada's statutes call it a deed upon death. NRS 111.671 lets the owner of an interest in property convey it to one beneficiary or several, with the deed taking effect only when the owner dies. The rules sit in NRS 111.655 to 111.699.

The model form in NRS 111.695 tells you most of what you need to know. The deed is revocable, it transfers no ownership until the grantor dies, and it revokes all earlier deeds upon death for the same real property. It must be signed, notarized and recorded with the county recorder before the owner dies, or it does nothing.

The form lists the county, city and legal description of the property, so copy those details from your current vesting deed. A typo in the legal description tends to surface years later, when the beneficiary tries to sell.

What the owner can still do while alive

Nearly everything. During the owner's lifetime a deed upon death does not affect the owner's rights, including the right to transfer or encumber the property (NRS 111.685). The beneficiary gets no legal or equitable interest while the owner is alive.

The same section lists other things the deed does not do:

  • It does not affect any other permitted method of transferring the property.
  • It does not reduce the rights of the owner's secured or unsecured creditors, even if they know about it.
  • It does not affect the owner's or the beneficiary's eligibility for public assistance.
  • It does not expose the property to claims by the beneficiary's creditors.

Changing your mind is simple. Under NRS 111.677, if the owner transfers the property to someone else during life, the deed upon death is void. If the owner records more than one deed upon death for the same property, the last one recorded before death is the effective deed, so recording a new deed is a practical way to change beneficiaries.

What must happen after the owner dies

The beneficiary must record a Death of Grantor Affidavit. On the death of the last grantor, a declaration of value (the form under NRS 375.060) and a copy of each grantor's death certificate must be attached to the affidavit and recorded in the office of the county recorder where the deed was recorded (NRS 111.699).

The affidavit identifies the deceased as the person named in the deed, gives the recording details of the deed and the property description, and states that the signer is a beneficiary or the beneficiary's authorized representative. It must be sworn before a notary.

Recording matters for a sale. Under NRS 111.689(9), a person who deals in good faith and for valuable consideration with a beneficiary has the same protections as if the beneficiary had been named in a final order of distribution, provided the Death of Grantor Affidavit was recorded. Without that recording, a buyer or title company has less to rely on.

StepWho acts
Sign, notarize and record the deedOwner, before death
Record Death of Grantor Affidavit with death certificate and declaration of valueBeneficiary
Publish notice to creditors and mail it to listed partiesBeneficiary
Wait for the claim period, then sell or distributeBeneficiary
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Do creditors and Medicaid still have a claim?

Yes. A deed upon death avoids probate for that property, but it does not erase debts. If the grantor's probate estate cannot cover an allowed claim or a statutory allowance to a surviving spouse or child, the estate may enforce the liability against property that passed by the deed (NRS 111.689).

The notice job falls on the beneficiary. After the death, the beneficiary must publish a notice to creditors and mail a copy to the grantor's personal representative if known, the Department of Health and Human Services, and known or readily ascertainable creditors. A creditor then has 90 days after mailing or after the first publication to file a claim with the beneficiary, and a late claim is barred.

The Department has its own track. If it receives notice, it must tell the beneficiary within 45 days whether the grantor received public assistance and, if not, give an original waiver of claim for recording. If the beneficiary never gives notice, the property stays subject to the Department's right to recover assistance, and NRS 111.693 adds that the deed statutes do not limit Medicaid recovery.

When a creditor claim is rejected, the beneficiary has 10 days to send written notice by registered or certified mail, and the claimant then has 30 days to sue or the claim is barred.

Selling the house after the owner dies

Beneficiaries can sell, and many do. Once the claim period has run, NRS 111.689(5) lets the beneficiaries sell or distribute the property without personal liability for claims that were not timely filed, as long as they gave written notice to the Department of Health and Human Services and received the waiver of claim the statute describes.

In practice that gives you a checklist:

  1. Record the Death of Grantor Affidavit with the death certificate and declaration of value.
  2. Publish the creditor notice and mail it to the required parties, including the Department.
  3. Wait out the 90 day claim window and the Department's 45 day response.
  4. Give the title company copies of the recorded documents. A title company may treat the notices as adequate notice and is not liable for claims it was not told about.
  5. Sign the sale deed. A sale to a buyer is a regular conveyance, so the transfer tax in NRS 375.020 applies at $1.25 per $500 of value in a county of 700,000 or more people and 65 cents per $500 in a smaller county.

A beneficiary who does not want the house can disclaim all or part of the interest by recording a disclaimer with the county recorder under chapter 120 (NRS 111.687).

A missing or defective deed, or several beneficiaries

There is no shortcut around a bad deed. An unrecorded deed does not work, a void deed does not work, and a deed with a wrong legal description invites a title dispute. In those cases the property may have to go through probate instead. Our Nevada probate guide explains that path.

Several beneficiaries bring a separate problem. All of them hold title once the deed takes effect, so a sale needs their agreement and signatures. If one beneficiary lives out of state, is hard to reach or disagrees about price, the sale slows down quickly.

  • Check that the deed was recorded before death and that the recording details match the affidavit.
  • Gather death certificates for every grantor, not only the last to die.
  • Make a list of every beneficiary and a way to contact each one.
  • Ask the title company early what it will require.

We buy inherited Nevada houses as-is, including houses that still hold the owner's belongings or need repairs. Because we pay cash, there is no lender appraisal to hold up closing once the paperwork is in order.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Frequently asked questions

What is the difference between a deed upon death and a will in Nevada?

A recorded deed upon death passes the named property directly to the beneficiary when the owner dies, while a will usually goes through probate. The deed only works for real property it describes, and it must be recorded before death (NRS 111.671).

Can I sell my house after recording a deed upon death in Nevada?

Yes. The deed does not affect the owner's right to transfer or encumber the property during life (NRS 111.685). A transfer during life makes the deed void under NRS 111.677.

Does a Nevada deed upon death avoid creditors?

No. If the probate estate is insufficient, the estate can enforce liabilities against the property, and the beneficiary must publish and mail a creditor notice. Creditors have 90 days to file claims (NRS 111.689).

What document does a beneficiary record after death in Nevada?

A Death of Grantor Affidavit, with a declaration of value and a death certificate for each grantor, recorded with the county recorder where the deed was recorded (NRS 111.699).

Can a beneficiary refuse a Nevada deed upon death?

Yes. A beneficiary can disclaim all or part of the interest by recording a disclaimer with the county recorder (NRS 111.687).

How a Nevada tax sale works

A Nevada tax sale is the last step of a county process that starts with an unpaid bill and runs through a two-year redemption period, a deed to the county treasurer and a public sale. The owner can pay and stop the process at nearly every stage.

The lien comes first. NRS 361.450 makes every property tax a perpetual lien that attaches on July 1 of the tax year and ranks ahead of other liens. When installments go unpaid, the tax receiver publishes and mails delinquency notices under NRS 361.5648 and 361.565, then issues a certificate for each unpaid property. Under NRS 361.570, that certificate lets the county treasurer, acting as trustee for the State and county, hold the property for 2 years after the first Monday in June of the certificate year, unless it is redeemed sooner.

Date or stageWhat happens
July 1Tax lien attaches to the property
Third Monday of August onwardTaxes due; installments follow in October, January and March
First Monday in JuneDelinquent property goes onto a certificate held by the treasurer as trustee
Two years laterRedemption period ends; deed goes to the treasurer in trust
After the deedCounty commissioners can order a sale; notice by certified mail at least 90 days ahead

How long you have to redeem

The base period is two years from the date of the certificate, and during it the owner can redeem by paying everything owed. That payment covers the taxes, accruing taxes, penalties and costs, plus interest on the taxes at 10 percent per year from the original due date. The Clark County Treasurer publishes the current figures.

One point surprises owners: the property keeps being assessed during redemption. Under NRS 361.570, the owner must also pay taxes, penalties and costs that accrue after the certificate date, with the same 10 percent interest, assessed monthly. The payoff grows each year you wait.

Abandoned property has a shorter path. Under NRS 361.567 the tax receiver may use an expedited procedure for property found to be abandoned, and the certificate then gives only 1 year of redemption.

  • Normal certificate: 2 years to redeem.
  • Abandoned property under the expedited procedure: 1 year.
  • Notice by certified mail before a trustee sale: at least 90 days, or at least 45 days in the expedited case (NRS 361.595).

If you own a vacant house, check its status now. An empty house is the kind that can be treated as abandoned, and that cuts your time in half.

Can I still get the property back after the deed goes to the county?

Yes, for a short window. Even after the county treasurer holds the deed as trustee, NRS 361.585 lets certain people have the property reconveyed by paying the taxes, costs, penalties and interest, until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale. The Washoe County Treasurer repeats this deadline on its auction page and may withdraw a property before or at the auction.

Reconveyance is not limited to the owner. People who may redeem include:

  • The owner and the person to whom the property was assessed.
  • A beneficiary under a deed of trust or a mortgagee.
  • A judgment creditor.
  • A person holding a contract to purchase the property before it was conveyed to the county treasurer.
  • The Director of the Department of Health and Human Services if the owner has received Medicaid benefits.
  • A municipality that holds a lien, and any successor in interest.

The purchase-contract line helps sellers. A buyer who signed a contract before the deed to the treasurer can pay what is owed and take the property back out of trust. A lender or a family member with a recorded interest has similar rights.

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

How counties run the auction

Each county treasurer runs its own sale, so the format and calendar vary. Washoe County holds one real estate tax auction a year, usually in April. Bidders register before the sale, and the treasurer records a quitclaim deed within 30 days of the auction.

The county sets the opening bid. In Washoe it is the delinquent taxes, assessments, costs, interest and penalties, or the assessed valuation, whichever is greater. Assessed value is about 35 percent of appraised value, so in some cases it exceeds the tax debt. The county only wants to recover what is owed, and buyers must investigate the property for themselves.

Nye County runs online-only tax sale auctions, and the Clark County Treasurer posts a trustee auction parcel list that changes often, with parcels crossed out when they are no longer eligible. A parcel can drop off the list quickly when someone pays.

NRS 361.595 sets the sale notice rules. Notice must be posted in at least three public places, including the courthouse and the property, at least 20 days ahead, or published for four weeks. Separately, the owner and any lienholders of record get certified mail at least 90 days before the sale. The buyer receives a quitclaim deed, and the treasurer records it at the buyer's expense.

Surplus money if the property sells for more than the tax debt

The surplus belongs to the former owner or lienholders, but only if someone claims it in time. NRS 361.610 sets the order of payment, and a missed deadline sends the money to the county.

  1. The treasurer pays the taxes and costs on that parcel first.
  2. From the excess, the county general fund takes the first $300 and 10 percent of the next $10,000.
  3. The remainder goes into a separate interest-bearing account.
  4. A written claim must be made within 1 year after the treasurer's deed is recorded. After that, the money goes to the county general fund and cannot be refunded to the former owner.

The treasurer must approve or deny a claim within 30 days after the claim period ends. Lienholders such as lenders and certain associations rank ahead of the owner in the payment order. If more than one person claims, the matter goes to mediation, then to a hearing or an interpleader action. An aggrieved person has 90 days to seek judicial review in district court.

Be careful with anyone who offers to recover surplus funds for a fee. A recovery agreement must be in writing and signed, and for a natural person's primary residence the fee cannot exceed 10 percent of the remaining excess proceeds.

Can a city or county take the property without a sale?

In some cases, yes. NRS 361.603 lets a local government or the Nevada System of Higher Education apply to the board of county commissioners to acquire property held in trust, if a public purpose is served. The treasurer then sends notice of intent to sell to the last known owner or heirs.

The owner has 90 days after that notice to redeem by paying the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs. If the owner does not, the treasurer transfers the property to the local government for the amount of the delinquent taxes. When the transfer is for street, sewer or drainage use, for a program to rehabilitate abandoned residential properties, or for open space, the delinquent taxes need not be paid at all.

Because the notice goes to the last known owner or heirs, an outdated mailing address is a real risk. If you own a house you are not living in, keep your address current with the treasurer.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling before the tax sale

The cleanest way is to close a sale while the property is still in your name or in redemption, and pay the county from the proceeds. Because the tax lien outranks other liens, a title company will require the balance cleared before it insures a buyer.

A cash purchase can move on a shorter clock than a financed one, since it skips lender appraisal and underwriting. The sequence is simple:

  • Ask the county treasurer for a written payoff figure, with the interest and costs through your expected closing date.
  • Find out whether the property is still in the redemption period or already deeded to the treasurer as trustee, because the deadline and the people who can redeem differ.
  • Sign the purchase contract and date it clearly. The redemption right for a contract holder applies to a contract made before the property was conveyed to the treasurer.
  • Close, pay the treasurer, and collect what is left of your equity.

If the sale price is above the debt, you keep the difference. At auction, the surplus claim process above applies instead, with a one year claim limit and county fees taken off first. We buy Nevada houses as-is and will give you a straight read on whether the timeline can work.

Frequently asked questions

What does a Nevada county tax sale sell?

It sells property that the county treasurer holds in trust after the redemption period ends. The treasurer delivers a quitclaim deed to the buyer under NRS 361.595, and the county's goal is to recover the delinquent taxes, penalties, interest and costs.

Can I stop a Nevada tax sale by paying?

Yes. Under NRS 361.585 the owner and certain others can have the property reconveyed by paying the taxes, costs, penalties and interest until 5 p.m. on the third business day before the sale.

How much interest accrues on delinquent Nevada property tax?

Interest on the taxes accrues at 10 percent per year, assessed monthly, from the date due until paid (NRS 361.570). The Clark County Treasurer uses the same rate.

Do I get money if my Nevada house sells at a tax auction for more than I owed?

Possibly. After taxes and costs, the county takes the first $300 and 10 percent of the next $10,000, and the rest is held for claims. A written claim must be filed within 1 year after the deed is recorded (NRS 361.610).

Is the Nevada tax sale redemption period always two years?

No. The certificate allows 2 years to redeem, but NRS 361.570 gives only 1 year for property determined to be abandoned under the expedited procedure in NRS 361.567.

Nevada Estate and Inheritance Tax: What Heirs Owe When Selling

Nevada estate tax and inheritance tax

Nevada's estate tax exists in the statutes, yet nothing has been collected on deaths after 2004. Under NRS 375A.100 the tax equals the largest credit the federal estate tax allows for state death taxes. Because it rides on that federal credit, it is called a "pickup" tax.

A Nevada return was needed only when the decedent owned Nevada property, died by December 31, 2004, and had an estate big enough for a federal return. Deaths from January 1, 2005 onward need no Nevada filing, and that stays true until the IRS brings back the old death tax credit. There is no separate inheritance tax in Nevada. The only state death tax is the NRS 375A estate tax, and nobody is paying it.

The federal estate tax

Only the federal tax is likely to touch a family. For someone who dies in 2026, a federal return is required once the estate passes $15,000,000. The 2025 tax law set that figure and it rises with inflation. The 2025 exemption was $13.99 million.

Most estates fall well below it and owe nothing federally. If yours is near or above the line, bring in a probate attorney and a CPA before you sell, because the federal return can shape what happens to the proceeds.

Quick reference

TopicRule
State estate tax lawNRS 375A.100, equal to the federal credit for state death taxes
State filing, deaths on or before December 31, 2004Required if the estate met the federal return level
State filing, deaths on or after January 1, 2005Not required
Federal filing threshold, 2026 death$15,000,000
Small estate set aside without administrationEstate not over $150,000 (NRS 146)
Transfer tax on a sale$1.95 per $500 of value, plus county add-ons
Department of Taxation phone(775) 684-2000
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

If the old Nevada estate tax applied

Where an estate did owe Nevada tax, the statute was harsh, and a leftover problem can surface when the house is sold years later. Payment came due at death and went delinquent nine months on. The personal representative paid from assets he or she controlled, and the debt stayed until satisfied.

The statute adds several consequences:

  • A lien on the gross estate arises at death and remains until the tax, interest and penalties are paid or the lien is discharged.
  • Whoever held gross estate property at death becomes personally liable if the tax goes unpaid when due.
  • Filing late costs a penalty of 5% of the tax for each month, capped at 25%.
  • Property sold to a bona fide purchaser or a security interest holder is free of the lien, yet the lien follows the sale proceeds.
  • The Department can start collection within 10 years after a determination of deficiency is issued.

Only deaths before 2005 are affected. Should a title company find an old Nevada estate tax lien on an inherited house, get a payoff or release from the Department of Taxation before closing. The Department's number is (775) 684-2000.

What heirs pay when they sell an inherited house

Expect the Real Property Transfer Tax, which the County Recorder collects at the time the deed is recorded. Every county charges $1.95 per $500 of value. Washoe and Churchill counties tack on $0.10 and Clark County tacks on $0.60.

Both sides are liable, jointly and separately, so write into the contract who pays. The deed travels with a Declaration of Value. Nevada recognizes 14 exemptions, and these are the ones families run into:

  • A transfer without consideration to the remaining joint tenant or tenant in common.
  • A transfer between persons related within the first degree of lineal consanguinity or affinity.
  • A transfer to or from a trust without consideration, if a certificate of trust is present.
  • A deed upon death that becomes effective at the grantor's death under NRS 111.109.

Heirs who sell to an outside buyer make a transfer for value. It is taxed even when the earlier transfer from the decedent was exempt. Remember too that property tax keeps accruing while the estate stays open.

Is probate needed before selling?

The answer starts with the title. A deed upon death on record lets the house skip probate. A house held in one name without such a deed normally needs a court case first.

A Nevada deed upon death works only at the owner's death, the owner can cancel it any time before then, and it has to be recorded while the owner lives. When several are recorded, the latest one on record before death wins. Afterward the beneficiary records an affidavit of death along with the required papers. Liens that existed at death stay attached, and the statute provides a way to notify creditors and file claims.

Two other statutes affect an estate with real property:

  • Under NRS 146 a court can set aside an estate of $150,000 or less without administration. The quicker affidavit route, available after 40 days, is closed to estates that include real property (NRS 146.080).
  • NRS 143 sets out what a personal representative may do. One with limited authority cannot sell or exchange real property unless the court is supervising.

Each estate differs, so let a Nevada probate attorney confirm the path before you fix a closing date.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Steps for an heir who wants to sell

A rough order of work keeps a Nevada estate sale from stalling.

  1. Find out whether a deed upon death is on record. If it is, the beneficiary records an affidavit of death and can move toward a sale without a court case.
  2. If there is no such deed, check the estate's size. An estate of $150,000 or less can be set aside by court order, and anything larger usually needs a personal representative.
  3. Ask the title company to search for liens, including any old Nevada estate tax lien if the death came before 2005.
  4. Decide in the contract who pays the transfer tax, and prepare the Declaration of Value.
  5. Keep paying or tracking the property tax installments until the deed is recorded in the buyer's name.

How a cash sale helps an estate

Selling for cash can cut the months an estate spends paying for an empty house. Cash Home Buyers buys Nevada houses as-is: no commission, no repairs, no seller closing costs, and a written offer. When an unpaid property tax installment or an old lien appears on title, the title company settles it out of the proceeds.

Before agreeing to a sale, collect the death certificate, the deed or title details, the newest tax bill and any court letters. Then check the rules and amounts with the Department of Taxation, the County Recorder and your attorney. What you read here is general information, not legal or tax advice.

Frequently asked questions

Does Nevada charge an estate tax?

On paper yes, in practice no. NRS 375A.100 ties the tax to the federal credit, and deaths on or after January 1, 2005 require no Nevada filing.

Does Nevada have an inheritance tax?

No. The sole state death tax is the NRS 375A estate tax, which is currently not collected.

What is the federal estate tax threshold for 2026?

A federal return is required for a 2026 death when the estate exceeds $15,000,000. Smaller estates owe no federal estate tax.

Do heirs pay transfer tax when selling an inherited house in Nevada?

Usually, yes, when the house goes to a buyer. Statewide it is $1.95 per $500 of value, Clark County adds $0.60, and both parties are liable. A deed upon death is one of the exempt transfers.

Can I sell an inherited Nevada house without probate?

Sometimes. If a deed upon death is recorded, the house passes without probate. Without one, an estate up to $150,000 can be set aside by court order, and bigger estates generally call for a personal representative.

Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property

Cash Home Buyers in Nevada

  • No fees, commissions or closing costs on a Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property sale
  • Turn the Nevada Probate Process and Selling Inherited Property offer down and you owe us nothing

Selling a Nevada House? Get a Cash Offer

We buy as-is.

Call or Text  (424) 435-2326


Last updated November 14, 2026.

Selling in Nevada?
We buy Nevada houses as-is, with no commission, no repairs and no closing costs to you.
Get My Cash Offer →

Estate size and the probate route

Nevada has four routes, and the estate's value and whether it includes real property decide which one fits. A house is real property, so most inherited homes cannot use the simple affidavit route.

RouteLimitMain condition
Affidavit for transfer (NRS 146.080)$150,000 for a surviving spouse, $25,000 for any other claimantDecedent left no real property in Nevada; 40 days after death
Set aside without administration (NRS 146.070)Estate of $150,000 or lessCourt petition; may not begin until 30 days after death
Summary administration (NRS 145.040)Gross value after encumbrances of $500,000 or lessCourt may order it if advisable
Regular administration (NRS Title 12)Above those limitsFull court supervision

The $500,000 summary limit reflects the 2025 amendment to chapter 145. Check the date on any statute copy you rely on, since older copies carry a lower figure.

In the set-aside route, value is fair market value minus enforceable liens and encumbrances, measured at the date of death. A mortgage on the house lowers the number that counts.

Can heirs sell before probate ends?

Usually the person who can sell is the personal representative, whose authority comes from the court. The affidavit route in NRS 146.080 is closed whenever the decedent left real property, an interest in it, or a mortgage or lien on it in Nevada. So a house generally goes through a court process or passes by a recorded deed.

A deed recorded before the owner's death that takes effect on death is the exception, and NRS 111.109 covers it. For a house with no such deed, the first step is usually a petition for letters. The petition must list the property, the heirs and devisees, and whether the proposed representative has been convicted of a felony, as NRS 145.020 describes for summary cases.

Co-heirs should agree early on who will serve and on whether to sell or keep the house. Disagreement can slow the petition, and a creditor or other interested person can object to a sale at the confirmation hearing.

Court confirmation of a sale

In a supervised estate, a sale of real property generally must be reported to the court and confirmed before title passes. NRS 148.060 requires the report and petition for confirmation within 30 days after the sale, and the clerk sets a hearing with notice under NRS 155.010. Summary administration follows the chapter 148 notice rules for real property sales under NRS 145.070.

The main safeguards:

  • Appraisal. A private sale cannot be confirmed unless the court is satisfied the price is fair market value and the property was appraised within 1 year before the sale. The court can waive the appraisal, for example when the sole heir is the representative or when all devisees or heirs consent in writing. Assessed value can then support confirmation (NRS 148.260).
  • Notice of sale. Notice runs in a county newspaper for 2 weeks, three publications a week apart, and the court may shorten that for good cause to not less than 8 days. Publication can be waived when the right people consent in writing, or when the property was publicly listed for at least 30 days (NRS 148.220).
  • Objections and higher bids. An interested person may file written objections, and other bidders may offer more when an offer is presented, in which case the court may confirm the highest bid (NRS 148.070, 148.120).
  • Commission. The court must allow a broker's commission, and it cannot exceed 7 percent for improved real property or 10 percent for unimproved (NRS 148.110).

A private sale notice must say where offers are received and name a day on or after which the sale will be made, at least 2 weeks after first publication unless the court shortens it. The sale must happen within 1 year (NRS 148.240).

Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your Nevada house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Independent administration

A personal representative with full authority under the Independent Administration of Estates Act can sell estate property without the usual confirmation steps. NRS 143.380 lets the representative sell at public auction or private sale, with or without notice, for cash or on credit, on terms the representative decides, and the confirmation requirements do not apply.

One safeguard turns on price. If the representative decides the real property will sell for less than 90 percent of its appraised value, all interested persons must consent in writing before the sale goes ahead, and the court must confirm the sale. Confirmation looks at notice, the court's approval of commissions, the necessity of the sale and the effort to get the highest and best price reasonably attainable.

Full authority comes only if the will or the court allows it, and the will can restrict those powers.

Creditors and family rights

Creditors get a window to file claims, and the surviving family can have a right to the home. In a summary administration, the representative publishes and mails notice to creditors. Creditors must file within 60 days after mailing or first publication, and the representative then has 15 days to allow or reject each claim under NRS 145.060. A claim filed late is barred, except where the claimant never got proper notice.

The family has separate protections. Under NRS 146.010, a surviving spouse or minor child may remain in possession of the homestead and is entitled to reasonable support. NRS 146.020 lets the court set apart the homestead, and property set apart is not subject to administration. A homestead selected and recorded by spouses during the marriage vests in the survivor under NRS 146.050.

A representative must close an estate within 18 months after appointment, with exceptions for pending claims, will contests and unresolved tax amounts under NRS 143.037.

Disclosure and taxes on an estate sale

The 10 day seller disclosure form requirement does not apply to a fiduciary who takes temporary possession or title solely to facilitate a sale for a person who is deceased or incapacitated. NRS 113.130 lists personal representatives, guardians, trustees and agents under a power of attorney in that exception.

Transfer tax and property tax still apply. The county recorder collects the real property transfer tax when the deed is recorded, at $1.95 per $500 of value in most counties. A deed that becomes effective on the grantor's death is exempt under NRS 111.109. A Declaration of Value accompanies each deed.

Property tax keeps running while the estate is open. Installments fall due the third Monday of August and the first Mondays of October, January and March. In Clark County, any recorded ownership document removes the owner-occupied 3 percent abatement until a new postcard is returned, so an heir who plans to live in the house should send it back.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy Nevada houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling to a cash buyer during probate

A cash buyer can purchase from the personal representative like any other buyer, and the court rules above still decide what approval is needed. In a supervised estate, a broker contract creates no liability for the estate unless the court confirms a sale (NRS 148.110).

Settle these questions before accepting any offer:

  • Has the court issued letters, and does the representative have independent or supervised authority?
  • Is an appraisal on file within the last year, or will the heirs consent in writing to waive it?
  • Do the liens, taxes and creditor claims leave enough for the heirs after payoff?
  • Will the family keep any right to occupy the homestead until the closing?

We buy houses in Nevada as-is, and an estate sale is a situation we see. Terms depend on the property and the court process, and nothing here promises a price. A Nevada probate attorney should review the steps for your case.

Frequently asked questions

Do I need probate to sell an inherited house in Nevada?

Often yes. The affidavit route in NRS 146.080 is closed when the decedent left real property in Nevada. A house usually passes by a recorded deed that takes effect on death, or through a court-supervised estate with a personal representative.

What is the small estate limit in Nevada?

An estate of $150,000 or less can be set aside without administration by court order under NRS 146.070. The affidavit route allows $150,000 for a surviving spouse and $25,000 for any other claimant, but only when there is no real property.

How large an estate can use summary administration?

NRS 145.040 allows it when the gross value after deducting encumbrances is $500,000 or less, at the court's discretion. If the value later proves higher, the representative must petition to revoke it.

Does the court have to approve the sale of estate real property?

In a supervised estate, generally yes. NRS 148.060 requires a report and petition for confirmation within 30 days after the sale. With full authority under independent administration, confirmation is not required unless the price falls below 90 percent of appraised value.

How long do creditors have to file claims?

In a summary administration, 60 days after notice is mailed or first published. The representative then has 15 days to allow or reject each claim under NRS 145.060.
